items.title: Reassembling Distributed Risk: Trajectory-Conditioned Action Generation for Multi-Turn Agent Safety
items.one_liner: ReDiR injects compressed trajectory-level safety representations during generation to block multi-turn distributed tool-use attacks below 8% success.
items.summary: Tool-using LLM agents can distribute a harmful objective across multiple seemingly benign requests and tool calls, allowing attacks to emerge only at the trajectory level. Existing defenses depend on auxiliary online reasoning or post-generation checks, adding high inference costs. The authors propose ReDiR (Reassembling Distributed Risk), a generation-time defense that compresses the active multi-agent trajectory into a compact latent safety representation and injects it into the base model. Evaluated across two agent-safety benchmarks and eight held-out tool domains, ReDiR reduces attack success rates to below 8% while preserving task fidelity.
items.bottom_line: ReDiR prevents multi-turn distributed safety attacks on tool-using LLM agents by conditioning generation on a compressed trajectory-level safety representation.

claims.text: ReDiR reduces attack success rates to below 8%, transfers to unseen tool domains, and preserves benign fidelity with low computational overhead.
claims.support_span: ReDiR reduces attack success rates to below 8%, transfers to unseen tool domains, and preserves benign fidelity with low computational overhead.

items.title: EMRB: A Multi-Level Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Reasoning over Raw Electromagnetic Signals
items.one_liner: EMRB benchmarks LLM capabilities in analyzing raw electromagnetic signals, exposing steep performance drops on complex system design.
items.summary: Large Language Models are increasingly evaluated on their ability to act as code agents, but their capability to analyze raw physical-layer measurements has remained unmeasured. To address this, researchers introduce EMRB (Electromagnetic Reasoning Benchmark), containing 200 problems across five difficulty levels and 27 question types derived from 11 raw I/O signal types. Evaluations across 14 LLMs showed scores dropping steeply from 84.9% on basic measurements down to 21.2% on system design. Furthermore, the proposed structured method 'ReconPilot' raised overall scores by 3.8 to 17.6 points across backbones by separating reconnaissance, analysis, and self-verification.
items.bottom_line: LLMs struggle significantly with raw electromagnetic signal analysis, though structured reconnaissance workflows like ReconPilot improve performance.

items.title: ToolMinimize: Auditing and Rewriting LLM Agent Tool Calls to Minimize Privacy Exposure
items.one_liner: ToolMinimize acts as a middleware to rewrite LLM agent tool call arguments, cutting privacy exposure by over 80% without losing validity.
items.summary: LLM agents routinely include privacy-sensitive data (PSD) in tool call arguments beyond what is required, crossing trust boundaries to third-party services. Measurements show 81-88% of default tool calls include unnecessary PSD, dropping only to 36-76% with explicit instructions. Researchers introduce ToolMinimize, a middleware intercepting tool calls to rewrite arguments to the minimum necessary data through removal, generalization, substitution, and truncation. Live validation on production models reduced privacy cost by 81.2-92.0% with 100% task validity and a median latency of 1.77 ms.
key_facts: Models tested: GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Llama-3.3-70B
items.bottom_line: LLM agents habitually overshare private data in tool calls, but automated middleware rewriting can strip unnecessary PII with minimal latency.

items.title: ACE: A Self-Correcting Agentic Canvas Editor for Multi-Slide Presentation Automation
items.one_liner: ACE combines a hierarchical scene-graph editor, content-aware routing, and self-correction to automate multi-slide presentations reliably.
items.summary: Commercial design platforms use LLM agents to edit documents, but legacy flat formats force agents to recompute coordinates and break layouts. The authors present ACE, an agentic canvas editor built over a hierarchical scene-graph with 98 specialized tools, paired with CARE (a content-aware router cutting input tokens by ~89%) and a self-correction loop driven by a ground-truth-free instruction-following judge. ACE significantly outperforms single-turn HTML pipelines on instruction following (4.23 vs 3.81) at 1.75x the speed and ~44% lower cost, with blind raters favoring ACE in 58.7% of decisive wins.
items.bottom_line: ACE achieves superior automated slide editing and layout stability by coupling a hierarchical scene-graph with iterative self-correction.
